x.ASV: The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem.

x.YLT: Words of a preacher, son of David, king in Jerusalem:

nt: The word **Qoheleth** is the name that the main speaker of this book chose to use for himself. In the original language it is a title that means “one who assembles a group,” that is, someone who gathers people together in order to teach them. You could spell out how this name sounds in your language, as the ULT does, or you could translate its meaning, as the UST does with “the Teacher.”

x.ASV: Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher; vanity of vanities, all is vanity.
x.Darby: Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities! all is vanity.
x.KJV: Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.
x.YLT: Vanity of vanities, said the Preacher, Vanity of vanities: the whole is vanity.

nt: Qoheleth is using **Vapor of vapors** as a common expression of his culture to mean “the most fleeting thing of all.” In this expression, a word is repeated in the possessive form in order to express a superlative. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The most fleeting thing of all] or [Utterly temporary]

Qoheleth says **the whole** as an extreme statement for emphasis. He does not mean that every single thing without exception is fleeting. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [just about everything is vapor]

x.ASV: What profit hath man of all his labor wherein he laboreth under the sun?
x.Darby: What profit hath man of all his labour wherewith he laboureth under the sun?
x.KJV: What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun?
x.YLT: What advantage is to man by all his labour that he laboureth at under the sun?

nt: מַה יִּתְר֖וֹן לָֽ⁠אָדָ֑ם בְּ⁠כָל עֲמָל֔⁠וֹ שֶֽׁ⁠יַּעֲמֹ֖ל תַּ֥חַת הַ⁠שָּֽׁמֶשׁ

Qoheleth is not using the question form to emphasize that people gain nothing lasting from all their labor. Instead, this is a genuine question. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I wonder if there is any profit for a human in exchange for all his toil that he toils under the sun!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **profit**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [good thing that lasts]

Qoheleth is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

Qoheleth is using **under the sun** as a common expression of his culture to mean “in this life on the earth.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See the Introduction to Ecclesiastes for more information on translating this expression here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [in this earthly life]

x.ASV: One generation goeth, and another generation cometh; but the earth abideth for ever.
x.Darby: [One] generation passeth away, and [another] generation cometh, but the earth standeth for ever.
x.KJV: One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever.
x.YLT: A generation is going, and a generation is coming, and the earth to the age is standing.

nt: Qoheleth is referring to the whole cycle of human life by naming its two major components, one generation **going** and another generation **coming**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [People are continually dying and being born]

x.ASV: The sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to its place where it ariseth.
x.Darby: The sun also riseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to its place where it ariseth.
x.KJV: The sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to his place where he arose.
x.YLT: Also, the sun hath risen, and the sun hath gone in, and unto its place panting it is rising there.

nt: Qoheleth is speaking of the sun as if it were a living thing that could be **panting** as it hurried back to the place where it rises. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it goes back quickly to rise there again]

x.ASV: The wind goeth toward the south, and turneth about unto the north; it turneth about continually in its course, and the wind returneth again to its circuits.
x.Darby: The wind goeth towards the south, and turneth about towards the north: it turneth about continually, and the wind returneth again to its circuits.
x.KJV: The wind goeth toward the south, and turneth about unto the north; it whirleth about continually, and the wind returneth again according to his circuits.
x.YLT: Going unto the south, and turning round unto the north, turning round, turning round, the wind is going, and by its circuits the wind hath returned.

nt: Qoheleth is referring to all directions by naming two major components, **south** and **north**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in every direction]
הוֹלֵ֣ךְ הָ⁠ר֔וּחַ וְ⁠עַל סְבִיבֹתָ֖י⁠ו שָׁ֥ב הָ⁠רֽוּחַ

Qoheleth is speaking of **the wind** as if it were a living thing that could choose where to travel and then decide to return the same way. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the wind simply blows around and around in the same course]

x.ASV: All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full; unto the place whither the rivers go, thither they go again.
x.Darby: All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full: unto the place whither the rivers go, thither they go again.
x.KJV: All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again.
x.YLT: All the streams are going unto the sea, and the sea is not full; unto a place whither the streams are going, thither they are turning back to go.

x.ASV: All things are full of weariness; man cannot utter it: the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
x.Darby: All things are full of toil; none can express it. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
x.KJV: All things are full of labour; man cannot utter it: the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
x.YLT: All these things are wearying; a man is not able to speak, the eye is not satisfied by seeing, nor filled is the ear from hearing.

nt: The expression **is not filled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and an ear does not fill up]

Qoheleth says **All the things are wearisome** and **a person is not able to speak** as extreme statements for emphasis. He means that the endless repetition he has been describing is exhausting to consider and that no one could ever finish describing how wearisome these things are. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [Very many things indeed are wearisome; a person could never finish describing them]

Qoheleth is not referring to a specific **person**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [anyone]
לֹא תִשְׂבַּ֥ע עַ֨יִן֙ לִ⁠רְא֔וֹת וְ⁠לֹא תִמָּלֵ֥א אֹ֖זֶן מִ⁠שְּׁמֹֽעַ

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [People are never satisfied by anything they see or hear]

x.ASV: That which hath been is that which shall be; and that which hath been done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun.
x.Darby: That which hath been is that which shall be; and that which hath been done is that which will be done: and there is nothing new under the sun.
x.KJV: The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun.
x.YLT: What is that which hath been? it is that which is, and what is that which hath been done? it is that which is done, and there is not an entirely new thing under the sun.

nt: The expressions **has been done** and **will be done** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and whatever people have done, it that which people will do]
See how you translated the same expression in [1:3](../01/03.md).

x.ASV: Is there a thing whereof it may be said, See, this is new? it hath been long ago, in the ages which were before us.
x.Darby: Is there a thing whereof it may be said, See, this is new? It hath been already in the ages which were before us.
x.KJV: Is there any thing whereof it may be said, See, this is new? it hath been already of old time, which was before us.
x.YLT: There is a thing of which one saith: `See this, it is new!' already it hath been in the ages that were before us!

nt: יֵ֥שׁ דָּבָ֛ר שֶׁ⁠יֹּאמַ֥ר רְאֵה זֶ֖ה חָדָ֣שׁ ה֑וּא

Qoheleth is using the question form to make an emphatic statement, that nothing anyone points to is actually new. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is nothing about which one says, “See this, it is new!”]
The pronoun **one** refers to any person at all, not to a specific individual. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [about which anyone says]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that this thing is something new]

Here, **our faces** represents “us,” that is, the people who are alive now. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from before us]

x.ASV: There is no remembrance of the former generations; neither shall there be any remembrance of the latter generations that are to come, among those that shall come after.
x.Darby: There is no remembrance of former things; neither shall there be remembrance of things that are to come with those who shall live afterwards.
x.KJV: There is no remembrance of former things; neither shall there be any remembrance of things that are to come with those that shall come after.
x.YLT: There is not a remembrance of former generations; and also of the latter that are, there is no remembrance of them with those that are at the last.

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **memory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [anyone remembering]

Qoheleth is referring to people and events of every time by naming two major components, **the former times** and **the latter times**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people and events of every time]

x.Darby: I, the Preacher, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.
x.KJV: I the Preacher was king over Israel in Jerusalem.
x.YLT: I, a preacher, have been king over Israel in Jerusalem.

x.Darby: And I applied my heart to seek and search out by wisdom concerning all that is done under the heavens: this grievous occupation hathGod given to the children of men to weary themselves therewith.

nt: The expression **is done** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [all that people are doing]

Qoheleth is using **I gave my heart** as a common expression of his culture to mean “I devoted my mind.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [So, I set my mind]

The terms **to seek** and **to explore** mean similar things. Qoheleth is using the two terms together for emphasis, indicating that his investigation was thorough. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [to search out thoroughly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wisdom**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [wisely]

Qoheleth is using **under the heavens** as a common expression of his culture to mean “in this life on the earth.” This expression means the same thing as “under the sun” in [1:3](../01/03.md). If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [during this earthly life]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **business**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [something unpleasant that]

Qoheleth is using **the sons of humanity** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to human beings]

x.ASV: I have seen all the works that are done under the sun; and, behold, all is vanity and a striving after wind.
x.Darby: I have seen all the works that are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and pursuit of the wind.

nt: Qoheleth is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation here and in verse 16. Alternate translation: [and—pay attention]

Qoheleth is speaking of everything people do as if it were a **pursuit of wind**. He means that gaining anything lasting from these deeds is as futile as trying to catch the wind. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and as futile as trying to catch the wind]

x.ASV: That which is crooked cannot be made straight; and that which is wanting cannot be numbered.
x.Darby: That which is crooked cannot be made straight; and that which is wanting cannot be numbered.
x.KJV: That which is crooked cannot be made straight: and that which is wanting cannot be numbered.
x.YLT: A crooked thing one is not able to make straight, and a lacking thing is not able to be numbered.

nt: Qoheleth is speaking of what is wrong in the world as if it were a **bent** object that someone might try to make straight. He means that people cannot correct the things that are wrong with life. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [What is wrong in life—no one is able to make it right]

nt: See how you translated the phrase **my heart** in [1:13](../01/13.md)

The word **saying** introduces the words that Qoheleth spoke to himself. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

Here, **my face** represents Qoheleth speaking of himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before me in Jerusalem]

Qoheleth is speaking of his **heart** as if it were a person who could see. In this culture, the heart represented a person’s thoughts and understanding, and seeing something represented experiencing and knowing it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and in my thinking I have experienced much wisdom and knowledge]

The terms **wisdom** and **knowledge** mean similar things. Qoheleth is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [wise understanding]

See how you translated the same expression in [1:14](../01/14.md).
